extracted.intended_audience: science journalists and applicants to the NASW Science in Society Journalism Awards
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards used by the National Association of Science Writers to evaluate submissions to the Science in Society Journalism Awards, focused on investigative/interpretive science reporting that connects science to societal impact and is accessible to non-specialist audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Award Purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: "To provide recognition for investigative or interpretive reporting about the sciences and their impact on modern society."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets the programmatic goal: entries should be investigative or interpretive pieces that examine science in the context of its effects on communities and society, not merely explanatory pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative or interpretive depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative or interpretive depth — beyond press release / explanation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions must go deeper than simple explanations or press-release-style reporting; judges look for work that uncovers, analyzes, or interprets issues in a way that reveals new understanding or accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science + Society (social and ethical implications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Winners "demonstrated innovative reporting that goes well beyond the science itself and into ethical problems and social implications for communities and society at large"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entries should explicitly connect scientific topics to ethical concerns, public policy, community impact, and other societal dimensions; innovative ways of linking science to society are valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diverse perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: "Shaped by a variety of perspectives" enabling "more broadly relevant stories"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges favor work that incorporates multiple viewpoints (e.g., affected communities, a range of experts) so the reporting resonates more broadly and avoids one-dimensional narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity in topics, sources, audience and authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity in topics, sources, audience and authors considered "a critical component of excellence"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection emphasizes variety across subject matter, the backgrounds of sources and authors, and attention to reaching different audiences; diversity is framed as integral to quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility for non-specialist audiences
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work should be understandable and engaging to general readers rather than only experts; clarity, context, and avoidance of unnecessary jargon are implied expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Award categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Six categories: Books; Science Reporting; Science Features; Longform Narratives; Series; Commentary
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions are organized into these categories; entrants should select the category that best fits their format and scope (e.g., a book vs. a news series).

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection to social/ethical implications (implicit newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond scientific novelty or technical interest, stories that make clear connections to social relevance or ethical stakes are treated as more newsworthy for these awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from PR/commercial influence (implicit newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work should demonstrate journalistic independence and not be unduly influenced by institutional PR or commercial sponsorship; original reporting and independence are prized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovative reporting approach (implicit newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges reward novel methodologies, storytelling techniques, or reporting strategies that reveal insights conventional approaches miss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community relevance (implicit newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that matter to specific communities or demonstrate clear local/regional impact are considered strong candidates; relevance to affected people/community context is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original interpretation, not just translation (implicit newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entries should offer original analysis or interpretation of scientific findings rather than merely translating study results into plain language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Going beyond science journals (implicit newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work should not be confined to summaries of academic literature; it should extend reporting into broader societal contexts, public debates, policy implications, or lived experience.
